row.title: Jim Sulivan's Adventures in the Great Snow
row.author: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu

plot_extraction.response_text:
Jim Sulivan, an amiable man trapped in a violent marriage to the beautiful but bad-tempered Nell Gorman, storms out after she scalds and strikes him. On the road, he learns that his uncle is supposedly dying and travels through a snowstorm to visit him, only to find him recovering. Heavy snow then prevents Jim from returning home.

Believing Jim has killed himself, Nell sends servants to search for his body. They find a similarly dressed traveler whose face was destroyed in a fatal fall and mistake him for Jim. After the body is waked and buried, Nell quickly marries Andy Curtis.

When the snow melts, Jim returns at night. Nell and Andy, convinced he is a ghost, refuse to admit him despite his threats, so he sleeps in the cowshed. The next morning they summon a priest and pay him twelve pounds to banish the spirit. The priest’s ritual awakens Jim, and when Jim enters the house, the terrified priest strikes him with a bell and flees.

Once the mistake is understood, Jim is willing to leave Nell with Andy, but the priest insists that Jim and Nell remarry, while Andy receives a small penance for marrying a widow too hastily. The neighbors enjoy the extraordinary succession of a wake and two weddings.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written as a comic Irish oral tale, presented less as polished literary narration than as a performance delivered by an expansive local storyteller. Its framing as an “Extract” from the legacy of a parish priest gives it a mock-documentary pedigree, but the narrative voice immediately replaces formal authority with colloquial intimacy. Repeated addresses such as “your honour” imply a listener within the scene of narration, while formulas including “Well,” “sure enough,” “by my sowl,” and “at all at all” reproduce the rhythm of speech, keep the story moving, and create the impression of spontaneous recollection.

The most conspicuous stylistic feature is the dense phonetic rendering of Hiberno-English pronunciation. Spellings such as “dacent,” “illigant,” “plisint,” “ould,” “throuble,” “dhropped,” “wid,” and “sperit” encode accent on the page, while elisions such as “an’,” “iv,” and “afther” sustain a rapid conversational flow. The dialect is also grammatical and idiomatic rather than merely orthographic: constructions such as “it’s Mick Hanlon that’s in it,” “the man an’ the woman beyant,” “it’s too late you are already,” and “divil a taste” give the narration a strongly local syntax. Archaic rural vocabulary—“borheen,” “gossoon,” “bosthoon,” “spalpeen,” “wake,” and “Shrovetide”—further anchors the tale in an Irish Catholic peasant community. The representation is highly theatrical and belongs to a historical tradition of literary dialect; its exaggeration can therefore feel both affectionate and caricatural.

Sentences are typically long, additive, and loosely coordinated. Clauses accumulate through repeated “an’,” “but,” “so,” and “for,” imitating a teller who continually appends qualifications, consequences, and incidental details. Paragraphs often begin with “Well,” resetting the oral rhythm before the next episode. Balanced literary description is less important than momentum: events are chained together by coincidence, misunderstanding, and escalation. Repetition is central to the cadence, particularly intensifiers such as “mighty,” “intirely,” “complate,” “sure enough,” and “tin times,” as well as recurring speech tags in the form “‘says he’” and “‘says she.’” These tags are retained even when the speaker is obvious, because they function rhythmically, like beats in a performed anecdote.

Dialogue dominates the story and carries most of its characterization. Exchanges are rapid, combative, and built around literal misunderstanding. Nell mistakes Jim for a ghost; Jim mistakes her supernatural interpretation for drunken nonsense; the priest initially accepts the profitable version of events and then panics when the supposed spirit appears. Characters speak in emphatic formulas, comic curses, blessings, invocations, and mock-solemn oaths. Sacred and profane diction mingle continually: “God rest his soul,” holy water, masses, and the sign of the cross coexist with “the divil,” “by jabers,” threats of murder, and opportunistic bargaining. This mixture gives the dialogue its irreverent energy without wholly rejecting the community’s religious worldview.

The tone is broadly farcical, genial, and deadpan. Violence, death, exposure, mistaken burial, and domestic abuse are treated as materials for grotesque comedy rather than psychological tragedy. Jim’s injuries are described through homely comparisons—his nose becomes “as big as a pittaty”—and the unidentified corpse has a face like an “over-boiled pitaty” or a pancake. Such similes are concrete, rustic, and deliberately undignified. Hyperbole is constant: roars threaten to lift roofs, blows improve by “tin times,” snow nearly freezes and smothers travellers at once, and the priest promises to subdue the strangest ghost in seven parishes. The narrator’s matter-of-fact acceptance of these excesses intensifies the humour.

Characterization is schematic and comic rather than inward or nuanced. Jim is a good-natured but unlucky husband; Nell is beautiful, violent, self-pitying, credulous, and astonishingly quick to remarry; Andy is opportunistic and timid; and the priest is worldly, avaricious, and protective of his authority. Their traits emerge through repeated actions and verbal habits, not through introspection. Even grief is dramatized as egotistical performance: Nell laments that she, rather than the supposedly dead Jim, is the truly unfortunate party. The narrator maintains amused distance from everyone, allowing no character complete moral superiority.

Structurally, the tale follows a cumulative misunderstanding plot. An initial domestic quarrel drives Jim from home; bad weather traps him away; a disfigured body is misidentified and buried; Nell remarries; Jim returns and is taken for his own ghost; and the priest’s exorcism produces the physical recognition scene. Each stage is plausible enough within the story’s comic world, yet each compounds the absurdity of the previous one. Delays, digressions, and apparently incidental anecdotes—such as the piper who plays at the wedding and then dies in the snow—enlarge the social world while reinforcing the narrator’s rambling manner. Suspense comes not from uncertainty about Jim’s survival, which the reader already knows, but from anticipation of the collision between his knowledge and the community’s false belief.

The ending uses comic restoration rather than strict realism. Jim is made to remarry his own wife, Andy receives a minor penance, the priest profits from both the exorcism and the wedding, and the neighbours enjoy the entertainment of a wake and two marriages. The final irony lies in communal silence: no one mentions the priest’s twelve-pound fee because he has forbidden discussion of the affair. This closes the story with an anti-clerical wink, exposing clerical greed and social hypocrisy while preserving the priest’s practical authority. Overall, the style combines dialect performance, episodic plotting, grotesque physical humour, religious satire, verbal repetition, and the communal perspective of folklore. Its chief effect is that of a lively fireside anecdote whose pleasure lies as much in the teller’s voice and comic timing as in the mistaken-death plot itself.

generation.response_text:
### THE MAN THAT CAME HOME AFTER HIS FUNERAL  
*An Extract from the Recollections of the Reverend Father Molloy, late of Ballycarrick Parish*

Well, your honour, if ever there was a dacent, quiet, unfortunate man born wid a talent for gettin’ into throuble that was none of his own makin’, it was Jim Sulivan of Knockbrack; an’ if ever there was a woman that could manufacture throuble out of clear spring water, it was Nell Gorman, his wife.

She was the beauty of three parishes, no less. She had black hair that would shame a raven, two cheeks like June roses, an’ eyes so bright a man would walk into a bog-hole lookin’ at them. But, by my sowl, she had a timper that would sour new milk at twenty yards, an’ a hand as ready as a blacksmith’s hammer. There wasn’t a jug, skillet, broom, tongs, or three-legged stool in the house but had been laid across Jim’s head at one time or another.

Jim himself was as mild as a wet Sunday.

“Nell, darlin’,” he’d say, when she’d fling the dish-water at him, “sure, what’s the use iv destroyin’ the furniture?”

“The furniture!” she’d cry. “Is it the furniture you’re pityin’, you idle, drinkin’, good-for-nothin’ bosthoon?”

“I’m not drinkin’,” says Jim.

“Then you ought to be,” says she, “for it might put a bit of spirit into you.”

An’ if he took that advice she’d bate him for comin’ home wid drink on him, so there was no road out of it at all at all.

Now one bitter mornin’ in the tail of January, Jim was sittin’ by the fire atin’ a bowl of stirabout, as peaceable as a saint in a stained-glass windy, when Nell asked him where he’d put the turf-spade.

“It’s behind the doore,” says Jim.

“It is not,” says Nell.

“Well, then, it ought to be,” says Jim.

“An’ is it me you’re contradictin’?” says she.

“Divil a contradiction,” says Jim. “I’m agreein’ wid you complate.”

That was the worst answer he could have given, though, between ourselves, no answer would have been the right one. Nell snatched the saucepan off the fire, an’ the water in it near boilin’, an’ sent a splash of it over Jim’s shoulder.

“Holy Moses!” says Jim, leapin’ up. “Woman, are you boilin’ me alive?”

“I’ll teach you where the turf-spade is!” says Nell, an’ she struck him across the nose wid the wet dish-clout, which had a wooden handle to it for reasons known only to herself.

Jim’s nose rose up that instant as big as a pittaty, an’ as red as the Pope’s best candle.

He stood lookin’ at her, the water steamin’ from his coat an’ the blood droppin’ on his waistcoat.

“Nell,” says he, mighty solemn, “there’s a limit to Christian patience.”

“There is,” says she, “an’ I reached mine the day I married you.”

“Then you may have a holiday from me,” says Jim, takin’ his hat from the peg.

“Go on!” says she. “An’ don’t come back till you’re worth lookin’ at.”

“Faith,” says Jim, “if I wait till you think that, I’ll come back on the Day of Judgment.”

An’ out he went before she could reach the tongs.

He had no plan in his head beyond puttin’ the hill between himself an’ Nell, which is a plan many a married man has followed widout knowin’ where it would land him. The wind was cuttin’ from the north, an’ little hard grains of snow were hoppin’ along the borheen like white fleas. Jim walked on wid his hands under his arms, lamentin’ his nose an’ wonderin’ whether matrimony was rightly called a sacrament or only a long penance wid meals in it.

He hadn’t gone two miles when he met Mick Hanlon’s gossoon ridin’ a grey mare that looked more dead than alive.

“Is that yourself, Jim?” says the lad.

“It was when I left home,” says Jim, “but I’m not certain what Nell made of me.”

“Your uncle Teague is dyin’ beyant at Glenmore,” says the gossoon. “They sent word for you. He’s askin’ for you every five minutes, except when he’s asleep, an’ the people say he won’t last the night.”

“Uncle Teague dyin’!” says Jim. “The Lord stand between him an’ harm! An’ does he still own the fourteen acres by the river?”

“He did this mornin’,” says the lad.

Well, your honour, Jim was fond of his uncle, an’ the fourteen acres did no injury to the affection, so he turned for Glenmore, though it was nine long miles over the mountain. The snow grew thicker, an’ the wind drove it into his eyes, ears, mouth, pockets, an’ every other place it had no business to be. Twice he lost the road, once he fell over a sheep, an’ once the sheep fell over him; but at last, near dusk, he saw Teague’s thatch white under the storm.

He pushed open the doore, expectin’ candles, prayers, an’ the keening of women, but there was Uncle Teague sittin’ up in bed wid a bowl of broth in one hand an’ a leg of a chicken in the other.

“Jim, me boy!” says Teague. “You’re just in time.”

“For the funeral?” says Jim.

“For the dumplin’,” says Teague. “Your aunt has it boilin’.”

“Aren’t you dyin’?” says Jim.

“I was,” says Teague, “but I thought better of it.”

It turned out the ould man had eaten three pickled herrings, half a cabbage, an’ a dish of onions at supper, an’ mistook the consequences for his latter end. He’d sent messengers to every relation that might be mentioned in a will, an’ by the time they arrived he was as hearty as a fox, though mighty willin’ to be pitied.

Jim would have gone home next mornin’, for he knew Nell’s rage cooled in about two days if there was nobody convenient to strike; but through the night the snow fell as if the heavens had been shakin’ feather-beds. It was up to the windy-sills by daylight, over the hedges by dinner, an’ by evenin’ it had covered the road, the ditches, the carts, an’ one small cabin belonging to Widow Driscoll, who didn’t discover till bedtime that she was livin’ underground.

“No man can cross the mountain in that,” says Uncle Teague.

“No married man, maybe,” says Jim, lookin’ toward Knockbrack, “but you don’t know what I left behind me.”

He tried it all the same, but after half a mile he sank to the waist, an’ a drift came over him till only his hat was visible. Two men pulled him out by the legs, an’ Uncle Teague put him to bed wid a hot brick, a quart of punch, an’ strict orders not to be such a fool again.

So Jim stayed in Glenmore one day, then another, then six more besides; an’ there was no message goin’ over the mountain, for the snow had stopped every road in the country.

Now Nell, when Jim first went out, was in no hurry for him to return.

“He’ll be back when he’s hungry,” says she to her servant-girl, Biddy.

“He mostly is,” says Biddy.

The first night passed, an’ Nell ate her supper. The second passed, an’ she ate Jim’s share too, lest it be wasted. But when the third night came an’ there was still no Jim, she began to remember that he had been a good husband in many respects—particularly in the respect that he cut turf, milked the cow, fed the pig, an’ brought in every bucket of water.

“The unfortunate man has destroyed himself,” says Nell.

“Maybe he went to his uncle’s,” says Biddy.

“Don’t contradict me,” says Nell. “I drove him to his death, an’ I’ll never forgive him for disgracin’ me in that manner.”

She sent Biddy an’ two labourin’ men to search the lanes, the wells, the riverbank, an’ the foot of Carrig Rock. They found nothing the first day, but on the second, when the snow eased for an hour, they came upon the body of a strange traveller at the bottom of a stony hollow.

The poor man had slipped from the road in the storm an’ fallen head-first among the rocks. He was about Jim’s height, wore a brown frieze coat much like Jim’s, an’ had brass buttons on his waistcoat. As for his face, there was no judgin’ it, for between the fall, the frost, an’ the stones, it looked like an over-boiled pittaty flattened under a cart-wheel.

“It’s the masther,” says Biddy.

“It might be,” says one man.

“It couldn’t be anybody that wanted recognisin’,” says the other.

They found in his pocket no paper nor token but a broken comb, fourpence, a bit of tobacco, an’ a small medal of Saint Joseph. Jim had owned a comb, smoked tobacco, respected Saint Joseph, an’ was seldom troubled with more than fourpence, so the evidence was complate.

They carried the body to Knockbrack on a door taken from an empty shed.

When Nell saw the brown coat she gave a screech that frightened the hens off the roof.

“Oh, Jim, Jim!” she cried. “Is this how you repay me? Wasn’t I a good wife to you, barrin’ a hasty word now an’ then, an’ maybe a harmless tap when you provoked me?”

“Indeed, you were,” says Biddy, for she wanted her wages on Saturday.

“An’ now I’m left a poor, lonely widow!” Nell continued. “Himself is beyond every throuble, an’ it’s me that has the sufferin’. He’s comfortable in glory, an’ I must look after the cow, the pig, the rent, an’ five acres of wet meadow.”

She flung herself on the corpse an’ wept so strongly they had to lift her off for fear she’d finish breakin’ what the rocks had spared.

The wake was the finest seen in Knockbrack for years. There were candles all around the bed, pipes goin’ in the kitchen, punch on the table, an’ plates of bread, butter, cold bacon, an’ currant cake enough to console the whole barony. Every neighbour came to praise Jim now that no answer was expected from him.

“He was a quiet man,” says one.

“Too quiet,” says another. “I never trusted a man that listened before he spoke.”

“He owed me two shillings,” says Darby Fennell.

“Whisht,” says Nell. “Would you blacken the name of the dead for two shillings?”

“I’d whiten it for half-a-crown,” says Darby, but she ordered him out.

Andy Curtis came to the wake on the second night. He was a broad, red-headed fellow of forty, wid a tidy farm, six cows, a new cart, an’ the courage of a lion where there was no danger at all. He sat beside Nell an’ told her not to give way.

“You’re young yet,” says Andy.

“I’m ruined,” says Nell.

“An’ handsome,” says Andy.

“I’ll never smile again,” says Nell, smilin’ a little to show him what was lost.

“Life must go on,” says Andy.

“It may go where it likes,” says Nell.

At that very moment a piper in the kitchen struck up “The Rakes of Mallow,” an’ the corpse, which had been badly settled on two stools, rolled half over with the vibration. Andy leaped into Nell’s arms, an’ Nell, thinkin’ it was grief that moved him, formed a high opinion of his tender heart.

The stranger was buried next day under Jim Sulivan’s name. Father Molloy said a handsome Mass, though he remarked afterward that he’d seldom buried a man whose widow watched the congregation more closely than the coffin.

Andy began visitin’ Nell before the week was out, to advise her about the cattle. Then he came to examine the roof. Then to inquire after the pig. Then to explain that a lone woman needed protection from designing men, of whom he was fortunately not one.

People talked, as people will when they have their own business finished, an’ Nell said she’d marry Andy merely to silence scandal. Andy said he’d marry Nell out of respect for the dead. Father Molloy said Shrovetide was near its end, an’ if they intended any foolishness they might as well regularize it while the church was open.

So, before Jim had been three weeks underground—or the man they called Jim, which was not the same thing—Nell Gorman became Mrs. Curtis.

There was another fine feast, an’ some of the neighbours complained they had hardly recovered from the wake. The same piper was hired, but on his way home he lost the road in a fresh snow shower an’ was found next mornin’ sittin’ frozen beside a hayrick, holdin’ the pipes under his coat to keep them warm. That made another wake, though not so expensive, for the parish had grown weary of currant cake.

Meanwhile Jim was still at Glenmore, playin’ cards with Uncle Teague, eatin’ his aunt’s bacon, an’ frettin’ for home.

At last the thaw came. The roads turned into rivers, the fields into soup, an’ the mountain path into a long black ribbon of mud. Jim borrowed a stick, put on his brown coat, an’ started for Knockbrack, not knowin’ he was dead, buried, mourned, replaced, an’ discussed from the pulpit as an example of the uncertainty of human life.

It was late at night when he reached his own house. A light showed through the shutters.

“Ah,” says Jim, “she’s waitin’ up for me. That’s affection, though she conceals it well.”

He knocked.

Inside, Nell was sittin’ by the fire darnin’ one of Andy’s stockings, while Andy drank punch in Jim’s chair.

“Who’s there?” says Nell.

“Open the doore,” says Jim. “It’s me.”

The stocking fell from her hand.

“Who?” says she.

“Jim, of course. Who else would be knockin’ at my own doore this hour?”

Andy’s face went the colour of cold stirabout.

“In the name of Heaven,” says Nell, “go back where you came from!”

“I will not,” says Jim. “I’ve walked eleven miles through mud, an’ I’m wet to the skin.”

“You’re dead,” says Nell.

“I’m tired,” says Jim, “which is different.”

“We buried you,” says she.

“Then you buried the wrong man,” says Jim. “Open this doore before I put my foot through it.”

Andy crept to the windy an’ peeped between the shutters. There was Jim in the moonlight, pale from the journey, his coat whitened with the last of the snow, an’ his injured nose still somewhat larger than nature intended.

“It’s him!” Andy whispered. “It’s the sperit of him, complate!”

“I hear you in there, Andy Curtis,” says Jim. “What business have you in my house at midnight?”

At that Andy dropped on his knees.

“God rest your soul, Jim!” says he. “There was no disrespect intended.”

“No disrespect!” cries Jim. “You’re wearin’ my slippers!”

Nell came close to the doore but kept the bolt fast.

“Jim,” says she, in a tremblin’ voice, “if you have any Christian feelin’, you’ll go away quiet. You had a beautiful funeral. There were four candles on each side of you, an’ Father Molloy said words over you that would have saved a Turk.”

“I don’t want words,” says Jim. “I want my supper.”

“You can’t have supper,” says Nell. “Dead men don’t ate.”

“This one does,” says Jim, “an’ if you don’t let me in I’ll make two more dead people before mornin’.”

At that Nell screamed, Andy shouted a prayer, an’ the pair of them pushed the dresser against the doore.

Jim battered at it till the roof shook.

“Open, you murderin’ woman!”

“Listen to him threatenin’ us from the grave!” says Nell. “Oh, the black villain! He had no consideration alive, an’ he’s worse by tin times dead.”

Jim might have broken in, but he was cold, hungry, an’ too weary to fight a dresser. So he cursed them both in a manner that proved he retained command of his faculties, then went to the cowshed, buried himself in straw, an’ fell asleep beside the brindled cow.

At dawn Nell sent Biddy runnin’ for Father Molloy.

She found his reverence at breakfast.

“Father,” says she, “Jim Sulivan’s ghost is in the cowshed, threatenin’ murder.”

“Jim Sulivan is buried,” says the priest, butterin’ his bread.

“He came back last night.”

“Did he, now?”

“He roared, battered the doore, an’ demanded supper.”

“A powerful, earthly sort of ghost,” says Father Molloy.

“He won’t go till he has me an’ Andy dead,” says Biddy, “an’ the mistress says you’re to come at once.”

Father Molloy considered the matter. He was a stout, comfortable man, very brave against sins, heresies, fairies, omens, an’ spirits that kept their distance.

“An affair of this gravity,” says he, “requires preparation.”

“The mistress will pay,” says Biddy.

“How much gravity did she mention?”

“Twelve pounds.”

His reverence put down the bread.

“For twelve pounds,” says he, “I’ll banish the strangest ghost in seven parishes.”

He dressed himself in his stole, took the holy-water vessel, a prayer-book, a candle, a small hand-bell, an’ his blackthorn stick in case theology failed. Two altar boys followed, though one deserted when he heard where they were goin’. By the time they reached Knockbrack half the neighbours had gathered behind them, each anxious to see the ghost exorcised, provided someone else stood nearest.

Nell met the priest at the gate.

“He’s in there, your reverence,” she whispered, pointin’ to the cowshed.

“Has he spoken this mornin’?”

“Not a word.”

“That proves the case is serious,” says Father Molloy.

Andy came from the house holdin’ a turf-cutting spade like a soldier who expected to be excused from battle.

“Would it not be better,” says Andy, “to burn the shed around him?”

“An’ the cow?” says Nell.

“The cow could be blessed afterward,” says Andy.

“Silence,” says the priest. “There’ll be no burnin’ until ordinary spiritual methods have been exhausted.”

He placed the people in a half-circle outside the shed, instructed them not to run unless he did, an’ began the ceremony. First he sprinkled holy water on the doore. Then he rang the bell. Then he said prayers in Latin so grand an’ rapid that the neighbours were greatly comforted, not understandin’ a word.

Inside, Jim slept through the first prayer, turned over at the second, an’ at the third got a splash of holy water through a crack directly in his ear.

He sat up.

“What thievin’ divil is that?” he shouted.

The crowd gave one great moan an’ moved backward six yards.

Father Molloy, though his knees disagreed with him, stood firm.

“Depart, unquiet spirit!” says he.

“Depart yourself,” says Jim. “I’m sleepin’.”

“You have no power here!”

“I own the shed,” says Jim.

“Tell us your name, apparition!”

“You know my name well enough. I paid you four shillings last Easter, an’ you said it was only two.”

At this the neighbours looked at Father Molloy with interest.

“That proves it’s a malicious spirit,” says the priest quickly. “No honest soul would keep accounts after death.”

He rang the bell three times, flung open the shed doore, an’ shouted, “Come forth, if you dare!”

Jim, who had endured about as much as a wet, hungry, wronged husband could, came forth immediately, straw in his hair, mud on his boots, an’ murder in his eye.

Father Molloy took one look, let out a cry that was heard at Glenmore, an’ struck him between the eyebrows with the hand-bell.

Jim went backward over a milk-pail. The brindled cow bellowed. Andy dropped the spade. Nell fainted neatly into Biddy’s arms. The neighbours scattered over the field like oats from a torn sack, an’ Father Molloy cleared the gate without openin’ it.

Jim rose, seized the bell, an’ ran after him.

“Come back, you ould robber!” he roared. “Is that how you welcome a parishioner?”

But when the people saw him limpin’, bleedin’, an’ cursin’ in plain Irish, their fear began to weaken.

“Ghosts don’t limp,” says Darby Fennell.

“They might if struck with a blessed bell,” says another.

“Nor they don’t leave footprints,” says Biddy.

Jim left plenty.

Darby came close enough to poke him with a hazel switch. Jim took the switch from him an’ broke it across his back.

“That’s Jim,” says Darby, rubbin’ himself. “I’d know the hand of him anywhere.”

Then the truth came out by degrees. Jim told of Uncle Teague, the snow, an’ his long delay. Nell told of the body in the brown coat. Biddy described the face that no Christian could identify. A messenger was sent to Glenmore, an’ returned with Uncle Teague’s oath that Jim had been eatin’ him out of house an’ home for three weeks.

Father Molloy was discovered half a mile away behind a stone wall, recoverin’ his authority. When assured that Jim was flesh and blood, he came back slowly.

“I perceived the fact at once,” says he.

“You perceived it after you struck me,” says Jim.

“The blow was diagnostic,” says the priest. “Had you been a spirit, it would have passed through you.”

“It near passed through me as it was,” says Jim.

Nell now began to cry.

“Oh, Jim,” says she, “what a wicked man you are to come home alive after lettin’ me bury you!”

“I never asked you to bury me,” says Jim.

“An’ what’s to become of me?” says Andy. “I married a respectable widow, an’ now she’s turned into another man’s wife under me.”

“That’s your own throuble,” says Jim. “You were always fond of bargains.”

Father Molloy raised his hand.

“This is a delicate canonical matter,” says he. “Nell’s second marriage cannot stand while her first husband is alive.”

“Thanks be to Heaven!” says Andy.

Nell turned on him.

“Don’t be too thankful, you red-headed spalpeen.”

“As for Jim,” continued the priest, “his wife has gone through the form of marryin’ another man, his own funeral has been celebrated, an’ a stranger lies under his name. There has been confusion enough to puzzle a bishop before breakfast.”

“Let Andy keep her,” says Jim generously. “I’ll take the cow, the pig, an’ my Sunday coat, an’ call it settled.”

“You will not,” says Nell. “Would you leave me disgraced before the parish?”

“You left me outside my own doore.”

“You were dead at the time.”

“I was not.”

“How was I to know that when you came at midnight?”

“By askin’ me.”

“I did, an’ you said you were yourself. That’s exactly what a ghost would say.”

Father Molloy declared that peace, propriety, an’ the good name of the parish required Jim and Nell to be married again, just to place the matter beyond dispute.

“Marry her again?” says Jim. “Haven’t I suffered enough from the first ceremony?”

“It’ll be only a short service,” says the priest.

“No,” says Jim.

“I’ll not charge the full fee.”

“How much?”

“Two pounds.”

“You charged twelve for tryin’ to banish me.”

“Spiritual work is dangerous.”

“It was dangerous for me,” says Jim, feelin’ the lump made by the bell.

In the end, as always happens, the priest had his way. Jim and Nell stood before the altar the following Tuesday, Nell in the same blue dress she had worn for Andy, an’ Jim with a bandage around his forehead. When asked if he would take Nell for his lawful wife, Jim looked toward the doore, but Uncle Teague was guardin’ it, so he said he would in a voice like a man consentin’ to transportation.

Andy stood at the back of the chapel, free again but not altogether pleased to see another man married to the woman he had escaped. Father Molloy gave him a penance of three rosaries for marryin’ a widow before her grief had properly cooled.

“Three?” says Andy. “Is that all?”

“Would you prefer twelve?”

“Three is ample, your reverence.”

Afterward there was another feast at Knockbrack, for Nell said she would not be married twice in one month without getting the use of the currant cake. The neighbours came in crowds, delighted with a household that had provided a wake, two weddings, an exorcism, an assault on a resurrected man, an’ enough scandal to last till harvest.

As for the stranger in Jim’s grave, they let him rest there, for he seemed as likely to be Jim Sulivan as anyone else, an’ the parish clerk said changing the stone would involve expense.

Jim an’ Nell lived together afterward much as they had before, only whenever she lifted the tongs he’d say, “Take care, woman, or I’ll die again,” an’ that generally stopped her for the length of a minute.

Andy Curtis never married, though he often said he would if he could find a woman who had been a widow long enough to be certain of it.

An’ Father Molloy kept the twelve pounds, of course, because, as he explained, he had successfully rid the cowshed of the spirit, for Jim never slept there again. He also forbade the neighbours, under pain of severe displeasure, to speak of the business, especially the part concerning the fee.

An’ that, your honour, is why every man, woman, an’ child in Ballycarrick knew the whole story before the week was out.

## The Roads That Remember

On the morning the road vanished, Mara Venn was carrying a jar of pear jam to her brother.

She had walked the same route every Sunday for eleven years: out through the blue gate, past the abandoned schoolhouse, left at the stone well, and then along the ridge until the valley opened below. Her brother’s farm lay at the far end, its red roof bright among the wheat.

That morning, however, the road ended at the stone well.

Not faded. Not blocked. Ended.

Beyond the well stretched a field of silver grass, unbroken to the horizon. There were no cart tracks, no milestones, no ridge, and no distant red roof. Wind moved through the grass in long ripples, making the earth look like a lake.

Mara stood with the jam jar tucked beneath one arm.

She knew better than to step forward.

In those days, roads had begun disappearing all over the country.

At first, people blamed poor maintenance. A lane near Bellweather became overgrown overnight. A bridge outside Merrow led travelers back to the bank they had started from. Then the northern highway, a stone road built three centuries earlier, vanished between two milestones, taking a mail coach and six passengers with it.

The government formed an Office of Roads Lost and Unreliable. Notices appeared in village squares:

TRAVEL ONLY ON VERIFIED ROUTES.

DO NOT FOLLOW UNFAMILIAR SIGNPOSTS.

IF A ROAD CHANGES BENEATH YOU, REMAIN STILL AND WAIT FOR ASSISTANCE.

No one explained what kind of assistance might reach a person on a road that no longer existed.

Mara set the jam jar beside the well and returned home.

She was a mapmaker by trade, though Bracken was too small to support such a profession. Most of her work came from land disputes, drainage plans, and farmers who wanted proof that a fence had been moved. She drew with patience and exactness. On her maps, every stream bent correctly, every house faced the proper direction, and every road had its measured width.

That afternoon, she opened the map of Bracken District and laid it across her table.

The missing road appeared in brown ink, running east from the well, climbing the ridge, and dividing at an ancient elm. One branch descended toward the river. The other went to her brother’s farm.

Mara dipped her pen and drew a line through it.

Road unverified, 17 Frostfall, she wrote.

Then she sat until dark, staring at the severed line.

Her brother Aron had been ill that autumn. Nothing grave, he had insisted in his last letter. Only a fever and a cough that lingered. His wife had died years ago, and his two sons had moved to the coast. If the road remained gone, he was alone.

At midnight, someone knocked at Mara’s door.

A young man in a gray government coat stood outside, holding a leather case.

“Mara Venn?”

“Yes.”

“Cartographer?”

“Yes.”

He looked past her into the house, where maps covered the walls like faded windows.

“My name is Elias Vale. Office of Roads Lost and Unreliable.” He opened the leather case and removed a folded document. “You reported the disappearance of the East Ridge Road.”

“I sent the notice this afternoon.”

“We received it before noon.”

Mara looked at him.

“That is impossible.”

“Yes,” Elias said. “May I come in?”

He placed the document on her table. It was her report, written in her handwriting, sealed with her seal. At the bottom, where she had written the date, the ink read 16 Frostfall—the previous day.

“I did not write this yesterday,” Mara said.

“We believe you.”

“That is not reassuring.”

“No.”

Elias removed several maps from his case. Each showed the eastern counties at a different time. As he arranged them, the country appeared to shrink. Roads vanished first, then villages, then rivers and hills. Blank spaces spread inward from the borders.

“These aren’t official maps,” Mara said.

“They are now.”

“What do the blank areas represent?”

“We don’t know.”

“Have you sent surveyors?”

“Many.”

“And?”

“Some returned.”

The fire cracked in the stove. Mara waited.

Elias continued. “Those who returned disagreed about what they found. One described a forest. Another said he walked through a city where everyone knew his name. A third insisted he had been gone for forty years, though only two days had passed.”

“And the others?”

“We found their boots.”

Mara folded her arms. “Why are you here?”

Elias took out one final map. It was old, drawn on yellowed cloth rather than paper. The ink had faded almost to gold.

At first Mara thought it showed Bracken District. Then she noticed the differences. The river ran farther north. The church stood where the blacksmith’s shop now stood. And east of the stone well, no road crossed the silver-grass field.

Instead, a narrow line curved south through a place marked Hollow of Bells.

Mara leaned closer.

“Where did you get this?”

“It was found in the Royal Archive, sealed inside a wall. We think it is at least five hundred years old.”

“The symbols are wrong for that period.”

“That is not the difficulty.”

He pointed to the lower corner.

There, in small, precise letters, was a cartographer’s signature.

Mara Venn.

She stepped back.

The handwriting was hers. Not similar. Hers. The long stroke of the V, the compressed second n, the tiny hook she always made at the end of a line.

“I have never seen this map.”

“Not yet,” Elias said.

Outside, the church bell rang once.

It was nearly one in the morning, but after the single chime came another, and another. Soon the bell was ringing wildly, as if pulled by panicked hands.

Mara and Elias ran into the street.

Half the village had emerged from their houses. People stood barefoot in the frost, staring north.

Where the church had been, there was now a pond.

Moonlight shone on black water. Reeds whispered along the bank. No broken stones remained, no bell tower, no footprints leading into the water.

But the bell continued to ring beneath the surface.

By dawn, the pond was gone too.

In its place stood a small meadow full of white flowers.

No one in Bracken could remember the priest’s name.

Mara remembered. Father Sel.

She wrote it down before breakfast.

By noon, she had filled seven pages with things other people had forgotten: the church windows of green glass, the crack in the tower, the graves behind the wall, Father Sel’s habit of feeding crumbs to mice. When she asked the baker about Sunday services, he frowned and said Bracken had never had a church.

“You must be thinking of another village,” he told her.

That evening, Mara agreed to work for the Office.

She made one demand.

“We find my brother first.”

Elias hesitated. “If his farm is inside the blank region—”

“We find him first.”

He studied her face, then nodded.

They left the following morning.

Mara carried measuring chains, chalk, a compass, notebooks, three sharpened pencils, and the ancient cloth map. Elias brought rope, food, two lanterns, and a pistol he admitted had never helped anyone.

Six villagers came to watch them reach the stone well. The jar of pear jam still stood where Mara had left it.

Beyond lay the silver grass.

Elias tied one end of the rope around his waist and gave the other to Mara.

“If the land changes, don’t run,” he said. “Running seems to encourage it.”

“Encourage what?”

“We haven’t named it.”

They stepped off the verified road.

For the first hundred paces, nothing happened. Mara walked with her compass in one hand and a pencil in the other. She marked their direction, counted her steps, and noted the wind. Behind them, the villagers became small figures beside the well.

At one hundred and twelve paces, the compass needle spun.

At one hundred and thirteen, the sky turned green.

At one hundred and fourteen, the villagers disappeared.

The silver grass rose around Mara’s shoulders. Though the air had been cold, summer heat pressed against her face. Insects hummed. Somewhere nearby, hidden in the grass, a woman was singing.

Elias stopped.

“Do you hear that?”

“Yes.”

“What do you hear?”

“A woman singing.”

“I hear my mother calling me home.”

The voice grew louder. Mara recognized the song. Her own mother had sung it while kneading bread, long ago:

Follow the road when daylight ends,

Follow the road through foes and friends,

But when the road remembers you,

Leave it before the sky turns blue.

Mara had always thought it a nonsense rhyme.

“Don’t follow the voice,” Elias said.

“I wasn’t planning to.”

The grass parted ahead.

A road appeared.

It was narrow and pale, paved with smooth stones. Wooden signs leaned on either side. One pointed toward BRACKEN, though in the wrong direction. Another read YESTERDAY. A third said ARON’S FARM: 2 MILES.

Mara’s heart tightened.

“That’s a trap,” Elias said.

“Probably.”

They followed it anyway.

The road climbed gently, though the surrounding land remained flat. After half a mile, they passed a ruined cottage. An old woman sat outside, peeling apples into a bowl.

She looked up as Mara approached.

“You took your time,” she said.

“Do I know you?”

“Not anymore.”

The woman’s face was thin and brown, her hair as white as milk. She held out a slice of apple.

Elias caught Mara’s wrist before she could take it.

The old woman laughed. “Still careful, Elias?”

He went pale.

“You know me?”

“I knew you when you were older.”

She returned to peeling the apple. The skin came away in one endless red ribbon.

Mara unfolded the cloth map. “Can you tell me where we are?”

“On a road.”

“Which road?”

“The one that needs you.”

“Where is Hollow of Bells?”

The woman pointed behind the cottage.

There was no path there, only silver grass.

“Why is my name on this map?” Mara asked.

“Because you put it there.”

“I haven’t.”

“Not yet.”

Elias stepped closer. “What is happening to the roads?”

The old woman’s knife stopped.

For the first time, her amusement faded.

“You stopped remembering where they went.”

“We have maps,” Mara said.

“Maps aren’t memories. Maps are promises.”

The woman looked toward the green sky.

“Long ago, people walked roads because they led somewhere. Then they began believing roads led somewhere because lines on paper said they did. The promise weakened. Now the roads are choosing for themselves.”

“Roads do not choose,” Mara said.

“Then why did this one bring you to me?”

The cottage door opened.

A little girl stepped out, carrying a jar of pear jam.

Mara recognized herself at nine years old.

The child stared at her solemnly. “Aron is waiting.”

Mara’s breath caught. The world tilted, and for one terrible moment she smelled her childhood kitchen: woodsmoke, pears, wet wool. Her mother’s hands were flour-white at the table. Aron, still a lanky boy, was stealing fruit from the pot.

She took one step toward the child.

Elias pulled the rope tight.

The vision broke.

The cottage had collapsed. The old woman and child were gone. Rotten boards lay in weeds, and the apple peel had become a red snake twisting in the dust.

Mara backed away.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

“Don’t thank me yet,” Elias said. “The road behind us is gone.”

He was right.

Only silver grass remained.

They continued forward because forward was the only direction the land allowed. The pale road twisted beneath their feet, sometimes stone, sometimes earth, sometimes black water firm enough to walk upon.

They passed milestones engraved with dates instead of distances.

3 Springrise, the first said.

Mara remembered that day. Aron had taught her to swim in the river. She had slipped from the bank, gone under, and opened her eyes to sunlight shattering on the surface. Aron’s hands had lifted her.

The next milestone read 28 Sunfall.

The day their mother died.

Then 11 Frostfall.

The day Aron’s wife was buried.

The milestones were not marking Mara’s life alone, she realized. They marked moments shared by her and her brother.

At dusk, they reached the Hollow of Bells.

Thousands of bells hung from dead trees in a deep valley. Some were iron and green with age. Others were silver, glass, clay, bone, or shell. None moved, though the wind had strengthened.

At the valley’s center stood Aron’s farmhouse.

Its red roof was covered in snow.

Mara ran.

The rope snapped tight between her and Elias, but he followed. They descended through the silent bells and crossed the farmyard. Chickens scratched near the barn. Smoke rose from the chimney.

Mara opened the door.

Aron sat at the kitchen table.

He looked older than he had in summer. His beard had grown long, and his cheeks were hollow. Yet he smiled when he saw her.

“You brought the jam,” he said.

Mara began to cry.

She set the jar on the table and embraced him. He felt solid and warm. He smelled of fever herbs and smoke.

“I tried to reach you,” he said. “The road kept bringing me home.”

“How long have you been here?”

“Six weeks. Maybe seven.”

“The road vanished yesterday.”

“For you.”

Elias searched the rooms while Mara made broth for her brother. He found no hidden people, no false doors, no obvious dangers. Still, he would not eat.

At nightfall, the bells began to ring.

Not together. One by one.

Each produced a different sound: laughter, weeping, thunder, breaking glass, whispered names. The farmhouse walls trembled.

Aron gripped Mara’s hand.

“It does this every night.”

“What happens afterward?”

“The house moves.”

The floor lurched.

Outside the window, the dead trees slid past as the farmhouse began traveling through the valley. It moved without wheels, gliding over the earth while bells rang above it.

Elias unfolded the old map on the table.

A new line was appearing across the cloth.

Golden ink spread slowly from the Hollow of Bells toward the west. It traced the route they had taken, then continued beyond the well, through Bracken, and toward the capital.

At its advancing edge, tiny towns vanished.

“It’s following us,” Elias said.

“No,” Mara replied. “We are drawing it.”

The map was a promise.

Every step she had measured, every direction she had recorded, had given the wandering road greater certainty. It was becoming fixed—and in fixing itself, it was replacing everything in its path.

She looked at her signature in the corner.

Not yet, the old woman had said.

Mara understood.

“This map isn’t from the past,” she said. “It’s from a future that folds back here.”

Elias watched the golden line advance. “Can you stop it?”

“Perhaps.”

She took out her pen.

The bells grew louder. Beyond the windows, fields, rivers, and villages flashed past, consumed by the moving hollow. Mara could see Bracken approaching in the distance.

She dipped her pen into black ink.

“What are you doing?” Aron asked.

“Breaking a promise.”

With one stroke, Mara crossed out her name.

The map screamed.

Every bell in the valley rang at once. The sound tore through the farmhouse. Windows shattered. Elias fell to his knees, covering his ears. The golden line thrashed across the cloth like a living thing.

Mara held the map over the stove flame.

Fire caught at the corner.

A road opened through the kitchen wall.

It was the East Ridge Road as Mara remembered it, lined with frost-covered hedges beneath an ordinary gray sky. At the far end stood the stone well.

“Go!” she shouted.

Elias helped Aron through first. The road shook beneath them. Cracks raced across its surface, revealing not earth below but fragments of other places: a summer ocean, a burning city, a room full of sleeping children.

Mara followed, clutching the burning map.

Behind her, the farmhouse collapsed into bells.

The road narrowed.

Elias and Aron reached the well. Villagers appeared beyond it, shouting and waving. Mara was twenty paces away when the ground rolled like a wave.

She fell.

The map slipped from her hand.

It landed on the road, still burning. The cloth curled, and for an instant Mara saw all the paths of the country shining upon it—not only official roads, but deer tracks, smugglers’ trails, forgotten alleys, the routes of migrating birds, and the invisible lines worn by people walking again and again to those they loved.

Then the fire reached the center.

The map became ash.

The road vanished beneath Mara.

She fell through cold darkness.

Voices surrounded her.

Turn back.

Come home.

You are almost there.

She saw every road she had ever taken. She saw herself as a child walking beside Aron, matching her steps to his. She saw her mother carrying bread to a sick neighbor. She saw Father Sel crossing the churchyard under green windows. She saw strangers traveling for weddings, funerals, work, forgiveness, escape.

Roads were not stone, she understood.

They were repetition. Intention. Memory.

They existed because someone left, and someone hoped they would arrive.

Mara reached into the darkness as if it were a page.

With one finger, she drew a line.

Not toward Bracken.

Toward her brother.

The darkness opened.

Mara woke beside the stone well with Aron kneeling over her.

The East Ridge Road lay beyond them, muddy and ordinary, climbing toward the ridge. In the distance, the red roof of Aron’s farm shone under the morning sun.

Only a few minutes had passed.

The villagers remembered the church again. It stood in its old place, Father Sel ringing the bell and complaining that everyone had missed morning prayers. Across the country, most vanished roads returned, though not always where they had been. The northern highway emerged beside the sea. A mountain pass appeared in the middle of a royal garden. The missing mail coach arrived in the capital three years late, its passengers insisting they had traveled for only an afternoon.

The Office of Roads Lost and Unreliable was renamed the Office of Roads and Remembrance.

Mara became its first chief cartographer.

She made new maps, but she no longer drew roads as firm, unbroken lines. She used softer marks that allowed for uncertainty. In the margins she wrote the names of those who traveled them, and the reasons they went.

Road to market.

Path to the winter fields.

Lane to the house where Lio Marren goes each evening to read to his blind aunt.

Trail used by children seeking blackberries.

Way home.

Years later, when Mara’s hair had turned white, a young surveyor asked why such details mattered.

“A road doesn’t care about names,” he said. “It only needs a beginning and an end.”

Mara looked east through the window.

The ridge road was bright in the late sun. Along it came Aron, walking slowly with a cane and carrying a jar of pear jam beneath one arm.

“No,” Mara said. “A road needs a reason.”

She went outside to meet him before the light was gone.
